lesson.title: De Brug Review
lesson.subtitle: the whole trail in one mixed drill: read, build and say the story

hook.title: The Final Mixed Set
hook.content: No new rule. Six old ones: a sch twin, a het word, a ch word, a book, a verb of arrival and a verb of going. The final drill is a test of recognition, not memory.

pattern.title: Every sentence is a return
pattern.content: Het schip komt aan, het huis is groot, de nacht is koud, ik ga morgen werken. Each sentence reuses a different part of the trail: a separable verb, an article, an adjective, a future.
pattern.trap_note: If a word looks new, check the pattern before reaching for a dictionary. The capstone is designed to be solvable from the trail alone.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (De Brug Review):
exercises.target_answer: het schip, het huis, de nacht, het boek, komen, gaan
exercises.meaning: ship, house, night, book, to come, to go
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "De Brug Review": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Het schip komt aan.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “De Brug Review”.

exercises.explanation: “De nacht is koud.” is word-for-word “The night is cold.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Every sentence is a return.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “The book is good.”
twist.explanation: The oldest twin in the course, read with the article it taught.

summary.outcome: Complete a mixed set drawn from all thirty topics.

summary.takeaway: Fluency is recognition made quick: the same handful of patterns, reused.

schip.etymology_derivation: English ship and Dutch schip are the same word; sch is /sx/.

huis.etymology_derivation: English house and Dutch huis are the same word; ui answers to ou.

nacht.etymology_derivation: English night and Dutch nacht are the same word.

boek.etymology_derivation: English book and Dutch boek share the spelling bridge; Dutch oe is /u/.

komen.etymology_derivation: English come and Dutch komen are the same verb; the vowel differs.

gaan.etymology_derivation: The same verb as English go, with the old g still pronounced.
